I was a consultant in the early 80's working on the transition / introduction of ATMs into the banking (RBC)industry. I ABSOLUTELY DISAGREE WITH YOUR STATS / GRAPHS stating the impact to the industry. The cost justification made to banking executives (by my team) stated that bank teller positions could be reduced by as much as 50% post implementation which the banks held us too. And if you don't have staff, then you do not need brick and mortar offices. Smaller communities were the victims of branch closures. The US was behind Canada in this transition and when I relocated to the US, I experienced this structural change first hand. First the bank (Wells Fargo) close it's local branch opening a service counter inside a grocery store. Then the service counter closed leaving the community with only and ATM and an 800 number that was rarely answered. I DO AGREE with your statement that a person's job is at risk of being replaced by another person who has the AI skill set to the do the job faster and "cheaper". But the employment predictions I've read and my personal in-industry experience has convinced me that we could easily see direct 30% job loss with the overly competitive job market left leading to a massive income loss for those left still employed. Finally, AI tools to write code are not new. In the early 90's, working at Motorola, I was using a "code generator" to auto generate COBOL code. It worked great. Then Motorola closed several IT departments across the US and Canada (300+ people) leaving just 3 of us to keep the ship running.
